podcast_episode.title: Ebola surge, AI math shocker and daylight saving time
podcast_episode.name: Ebola surge, AI math shocker and daylight saving time
podcast_episode.description: In this week’s news roundup, we take a look at what’s happening with the Ebola outbreak in parts of Africa. Later SciAm editorial fellow Peter Hall joins host Rachel Feltman to discuss recent claims by OpenAI and Anthropic that their models have solved some of the world’s toughest math and physics problems. Plus, we dive into new research that suggests making daylight saving time permanent could put schoolchildren at risk. podcast_episode.title: Why we’re still obsessed with vampires
podcast_episode.name: Why we’re still obsessed with vampires
podcast_episode.description: In this Halloween special episode of Science Quickly, host Rachel Feltman explores why our fascination with vampires refuses to die. We dive into the spooky history of vampires—from tuberculosis outbreaks in the 18th and 19th centuries to sexy pop culture icons—and examine what our collective obsession with them says about us. Recommended Reading: Exhumed: Unearthing the History of the American Vampire. Aaron Mahnke. podcast_episode.title: Cartwheeling snakes, vocal vultures and a mysterious Martian moon
podcast_episode.name: Cartwheeling snakes, vocal vultures and a mysterious Martian moon
podcast_episode.description: On this episode of Science Quickly, host Rachel Feltman discusses Japan’s half-billion-dollar mission to land on Mars’s lumpy little moon Phobos and catches up on animal behavior, both big and small—from newly discovered cartwheeling snakes to the surprisingly complex vocal repertoire of social vultures. We also explore how Japanese macaques developed food caution after surviving a disease outbreak and why adults are actually more creative than preschoolers (they just need more confidence). podcast_episode.title: Why your brain hates uncertainty
podcast_episode.name: Why your brain hates uncertainty
podcast_episode.description: Our brains are constantly trying to predict what comes next, but in an increasingly unpredictable world, that mental workload can fuel stress, anxiety and even depression. In this episode of Science Quickly, author Maia Szalavitz explains how the brain processes uncertainty, why some people are better equipped to handle it than others and how we can build resilience by learning to embrace the unknown. podcast_episode.title: Slime molds, Pompeii and alien consciousness with Annalee Newitz
podcast_episode.name: Slime molds, Pompeii and alien consciousness with Annalee Newitz
podcast_episode.description: In this episode of Science Quickly, science journalist and science-fiction author Annalee Newitz discusses their novel A Wall Is Also a Road, a story about a graduate student who also happens to be a conscious slime mold alien. The slime mold, named Gardenpath, has decided to study an alien civilization, and her fieldwork has taken her to Pompeii, where she befriends a local sex worker named Murtis. Newitz and Science Quickly host Rachel Feltman talk about the compelling nature of slime molds, the value of looking at human civilization from the outside and the ordinary people of Pompeii. podcast_episode.title: Cover Story: Escaping the Infinite Scroll
podcast_episode.name: Cover Story: Escaping the Infinite Scroll
podcast_episode.description: How much screen time is too much? In this episode of Science Quickly, Scientific American associate editor Allison Parshall reads her November cover story, “Escaping the Infinite Scroll.” In the story, she explores the growing debate over screen addiction and problematic social media use. From landmark lawsuits against tech companies to the psychology behind endless scrolling, she explains what researchers know about digital dependence, why social platforms are designed to keep us engaged and how some people are turning to addiction-style recovery programs for help.
